rationale: A `uses` edge over a link destination used to be indistinguishable from a `uses` edge over an unresolvable local reference. Measured on the 600-file prefix of the 17,456-file admitted population (production parseFile, validation/m60/markdown/abc-before-600.json): 4,107 of 4,951 targets binding to no local declaration carry a URI scheme — 3,996 https, 110 http, 1 some — so the unresolved column overstated this lane's defects by 82.9% and nothing in the output said which was which. The edge itself is correct and is KEPT: a markdown link to a website is a real use of that resource, and dropping 4,107 edges to improve a column is the opposite of the point. What changed is that the edge now carries `isExternal` and a `targetKind`. Seven behaviours are pinned because each is a place the obvious implementation is wrong. (1) The THREE-WAY split, not a boolean: `docs/guide.md` names a file in THIS repository, so marking it external is a false statement — it is a modelling gap and is counted separately. (2) A scheme of ONE character is a Windows drive path, not a URI. RFC 3986 admits `X:`, so `X:/src/lib.rs` satisfies the scheme grammar and the first implementation of this put it in the external bucket. (3) A network-path reference `//cdn.example.com/x.js` has no scheme at all and is still remote — the authority is what makes it remote. (4) The two legal WRAPPED forms are opposites, and pinning only one of them passes an implementation that gets the other wrong. `[x](<https://y>)` — CommonMark 0.31.2 §4.7: the angle brackets are the enclosing syntax and NOT part of the destination, so the target is `https://y`. `[x]((https://y))` — the parentheses ARE part of the destination, because CommonMark permits unescaped parentheses inside a bare destination when balanced, so the target is `(https://y)` and the scheme scan must see THROUGH them. The angle case was found by this fixture, not by reading: the analyzer published `<https://y>`, which src/ast/pool-worker.ts:653 then deleted at the production boundary, so `analyze()` emitted the edge and `parseFile` returned zero. (5) The classification reads the DESTINATION and never the label, in both directions: the fixture carries a label that looks exactly like a URL over a relative destination, and an innocuous label over a remote one. Classifying the label is the obvious implementation because the label is the text a reader sees. (6) An autolink is external BY CONSTRUCTION — `<https://x>` and `<a@b.c>` are the two forms CommonMark defines and neither can name a local declaration — while `targetKind` still separates a URI autolink from an email autolink. (7) Nothing about the endpoint or the label moved: the target string is the destination as written and the type is still `uses`, because mutant MD-L1 relabels these in place and markdown/internal-anchor-links forbids `uses` over an in-document anchor.

_declaredLimitation.what: The marker is COUNTABLE and nothing more. No production consumer reads it: `isExternal` on analyzer metadata has no reader anywhere in src/ (the `isExternal` in src/lsp/call_hierarchy.ts and src/lsp/graph_usages.ts is a call-hierarchy concept on a different object), and the store still attempts to bind every one of these targets and records it as unresolved. So the store-side resolution rate for this lane is unchanged by this commit.
_declaredLimitation.why: src/ast/parallel-indexer.ts is shared machinery (workstream §8) and is not this lane's to edit. The analyzer half is the half that can be done here, and doing it means the number is available to whoever wires the consumer.
_declaredLimitation.wouldBeWrongTo: report this as a resolution improvement. It is a bookkeeping change; the resolution rate moved 0.
